why: Two neighbouring length-k windows share k-1 elements, so equal sums force a[i] = a[i+k]: the array must be periodic with period k. Positions split into k residue classes (i mod k); in each class keep the most frequent value and change the rest.
hints: Compare the sum of window [i, i+k-1] with the window one step to the right. What must be true about the two elements that differ?
Equal window sums for every shift means prod_price[i] == prod_price[i+k] for all i. So every class of indices with the same i mod k must end up holding one value.
For each residue r in 0..k-1, count values at indices r, r+k, r+2k, ... and keep the most common one. Answer = n - sum of those maxima. O(n).
pitfalls: You do not need the common sum itself; any periodic array has equal window sums.
If k >= n there is at most one window, so the answer is 0 (every class has at most one element).
Changed values must be positive; using an existing value of the class always satisfies that.
statement:
You are given an array prod_price of n positive integers and an integer k. In one change you may replace any element with any positive integer.

Return the minimum number of changes so that every contiguous subarray of length k has the same sum.

Worked example: prod_price = [1, 3, 2, 2, 3], k = 3.

  • The window sums are now 1+3+2 = 6, 3+2+2 = 7, 2+2+3 = 7: not all equal.
  • Change prod_price[3] from 2 to 1, giving [1, 3, 2, 1, 3].
  • Window sums: 6, 6, 6. One change is enough and zero is not, so the answer is 1.

For [5, 7, 7, 8] with k = 2 the answer is 2, for example [7, 7, 7, 7].
constraints:
• Not stated in the source; reasonable bounds: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10^5
  • 1 ≤ prod_price[i] ≤ 10^9
